anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excess accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update/delete churn.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical read/write demand exceeds the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage subsystem.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources (file descriptors, async-I/O contexts, threads, shared memory, etc.) needed by the database engine and its workers.

When all three conditions coincide, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: tables and indexes balloon in size, causing every scan, vacuum, checkpoint, or log flush to issue more physical I/O against devices that are already saturated. Read and write latencies rise sharply, buffer-pool hit ratios plunge, and wait profiles fill with both I/O waits and kernel-level "resource temporarily unavailable" errors. Autovacuum or garbage-collection workers start and stop erratically as they hit OS limits on file handles or AIO contexts, further delaying cleanup. Administrators observe runaway disk-space usage, near-continuous storage queues, intermittent inability to start new backend or maintenance processes, and a mix of MVCC horizon warnings, I/O stall messages, and kernel denials in system logs. Planner misestimates and timeout-driven query cancellations become frequent, and parts of the workload may hang while existing sessions cling to old snapshots that prevent reclamation of space.

Causal chain: heavy OLTP churn creates surplus row versions, inflating on-disk structures and multiplying physical pages that must be read, written, and eventually vacuumed. This extra traffic pushes the storage subsystem to (or beyond) its throughput limits, lengthening I/O completion times. Prolonged I/O stretches the window during which cleanup workers must hold resources, so they consume more file descriptors, AIO slots, and threads; meanwhile other sessions also queue additional I/O, driving kernel resource counts higher. Once OS ceilings are reached, new workers or I/O submissions are rejected, which stalls or aborts garbage collection and checkpoints, causing even faster version buildup and still more I/O. The feedback loop—version bloat → higher I/O demand → storage saturation → kernel resource exhaustion → stalled cleanup—amplifies both performance degradation and risk of outage until manual intervention or configuration changes break the cycle.

entry.official_definition: Aborts any statement that takes more than the specified amount of time; zero disables the timeout.
entry.trigger_condition: A SQL statement runs longer than statement_timeout, measured from command arrival until completion.
entry.workload_impact: The running statement is aborted; when configured, the timed-out statement is logged.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
